synth.title: Search + browse findability
synth.principle_summary: Findability is a mechanics layer that sits under, and is distinct from, Solen's locked search/filter product decisions (single-select, AND-combine backend). Search and browse are not a mode users pick between but two channels most sessions mix (T2, Katz and Byrne 2003). Within that, three sourced mechanics make a facet/result system usable rather than merely present: (1) facet state should stay visible and legible before commitment, ideally as a live result count, both in academic recommendation (T2, Hearst 2006) and as an extremely convergent real-app pattern (CONV, "Show N results" on the commit button across at least seven current booking/commerce apps); (2) reformulation, not one committed query, is the normal information-seeking path (T2, Bates 1989 berrypicking), so facet/search changes should read as adjusting a live view, never a full reload; (3) a zero- or low-result state is the highest-risk moment in the flow and needs a structural recovery action, not just apologetic copy, both by directional research (T3, Baymard) and by near-universal real-app convergence (CONV, 12+ apps sampled share one recovery shape, and the strongest examples relabel a fallback result set as still-visible rather than wiping the screen). A fourth, weaker signal (T2 with an acknowledged hedge) argues the single most differentiating fact on a result row belongs top-left/early, but only on unstructured lists; Solen's photo-led card grammar is already structured, so this sets a placement rule for new text additions, not a card redesign.

real_world_evidence.source: Fresha search results page (fresha.com/search, live fetch this session)
real_world_evidence.what: Search bar is a single compound state-summary chip showing all three active facets inline at once ("Hair & styling | Tomorrow | Current location"), not a blank query box; results toolbar below it is 4 pill filters (all-filters / Sort by / Max price / Venue type) plus a small centered grey plain-text result count line ("21 venues nearby"), no icon, no bold.

real_world_evidence.source: Fresha, Zocdoc, eBay, Alan, FotMob, Glassdoor, Vivino, Shopee (Mobbin live-screen capture, cross-app)
real_world_evidence.what: Filter-sheet commit buttons restate the live result count in the label itself before the user commits: "Show 418 results" (Zocdoc), "Show results" (eBay), "Show therapists" (Alan), "Show 60 results" (FotMob), "Show 195 jobs" (Glassdoor), "Show 151 wines" (Vivino). Convergent across at least 7 unrelated booking/commerce apps sampled, none faked or single-sourced.

real_world_evidence.source: TheFork, Walmart, Too Good To Go, Tabby, Google Drive, Wise, ClassPass, HelloFresh (Mobbin live-screen capture, 12+ apps sampled total)
real_world_evidence.what: Zero-result recovery is a near-universal shape: icon/illustration, bold short headline naming the filters (not the content) as the cause, one line of grey subtext, one primary single-tap recovery CTA ("Clear filters"/"Reset filters"/"Start a new search"). ClassPass adds a second non-destructive path ("Add categories") alongside the reset. HelloFresh is the strongest example: instead of a bare apology it keeps a "Most recent recipes" fallback section visible below the empty message so the user is never on a true dead end.

Low-result days use an explicit reformulation nudge rather than an empty state: a horizontal day-strip stays visible, and a section header "Available on other days" relabels the remaining results as a fallback set instead of wiping the screen. This is a distinct, softer recovery technique from the hard zero-result empty state.

real_world_evidence.source: Booksy homepage, Treatwell homepage (live fetch this session)
real_world_evidence.what: Booksy leads with a browse-first icon-tile category grid (roughly 8 primary + 10 secondary categories) as the visual anchor of its entry screen; Treatwell leads with a treatment-level trending/social discovery rail ("What is hot on socials") ahead of any typed query, while keeping a search bar in the header. Fresha, by contrast, leads with the search bar itself. Three competitors, three different search-vs-browse balances, no industry consensus to copy.

Distance facet shows a live per-option count in parentheses next to each radio choice ("5 miles (11)", "25 miles (106)"), letting the user see result impact before selecting rather than after. Strongest single findability pattern observed, but requires real wired per-option counts, currently unconfirmed for Solen's Angebote facets.

Natural-language / AI-generated search query input ("Search with AI", "Filter Assist", conversational "Reply or search") is an emerging pattern in a handful of current apps, three data points, not a saturated convention. Explicitly a watch-not-build signal: Solen's search is owner-locked single-select with no chat/AI search surface planned.

synth.generative_prior: Concrete defaults for a first-pass mockup, each grounded in a real, sourced app pattern rather than invented: (1) the search/filter summary bar should show the current state of all active facets at a glance (Fresha's compound chip is the reference shape, T3), not a placeholder text box that hides what is already selected, echoing Hearst's T2 recommendation to keep filter state visible and reversible; (2) a filter sheet's commit button should restate the outcome before the user commits, e.g. "N Ergebnisse anzeigen" mirroring the "Show N results" pattern convergent across Zocdoc, eBay, Alan, FotMob, Glassdoor, Vivino, and Shopee (CONV), rather than a bare "Anwenden"; (3) top-level Angebote facet chips should fit one unscrolled row at the 375px floor with overflow behind a single "Mehr Filter" disclosure (number to be set by the Taste-Lab probe below, grounded in the existing TabPill component's measured width, not invented here); (4) the zero-result state needs an illustration or icon, a headline naming the filters as the cause (not the content), one line of subtext, and exactly one primary recovery CTA that relaxes the tightest active facet, mirroring the convergent shape across TheFork/Walmart/Tabby/Wise/Google Drive (CONV); (5) where results are merely sparse rather than zero, prefer ClassPass's technique of relabeling the remaining set under an "Andere Tage verfügbar" style header over wiping the screen to a hard empty state (T3). None of these defaults touch Solen's locked single-select policy or the AND-combine backend contract; they are the perceptual shell around that already-decided mechanic.
synth.proposed_addition:
DOMAIN: Findability (search + browse mechanics), new section for RATIONALE.md, target_anchor "new domain: findability". Suggested placement: immediately after the existing Domain 11 (enforcement) block, numbered by whatever the synthesis pass assigns next.

Search and browse are not two competing modes users pick between, they are two channels most sessions mix (T2, Katz and Byrne 2003, cited by NN/g: 70 percent link-first / 30 percent search-first in task testing). Real-app confirmation shows no industry consensus on the balance itself: Fresha leads with a compound search-state chip (search-first), Booksy leads with a browse-first icon-tile category grid, Treatwell leads with a trending-treatments discovery rail (browse-first with search retained in the header). This domain does not pick a winner among the three, it governs the mechanics UNDER whichever balance Solen's own traffic mix justifies, and under Solen's existing locked search and Angebote-filter behavior (single-select owner lock, AND-combine backend, already project fact, not repeated or reopened here).

**Facet state stays visible and legible, ideally with a live outcome count (T2 Hearst 2006, reinforced by strong real-app convergence, CONV).** Hearst's design recommendations call for showing counts before a facet is applied, keeping the current filter state visible and reversible, and never landing on an unrecoverable empty set. Current shipping apps confirm this is not just academic advice: filter-sheet commit buttons across at least seven unrelated booking/commerce apps (Zocdoc "Show 418 results", eBay "Show results", Alan "Show therapists", FotMob "Show 60 results", Glassdoor "Show 195 jobs", Vivino "Show 151 wines", Fresha's own toolbar count line "21 venues nearby") restate the outcome before the user commits, so the user chooses a result, not a guess. Zocdoc goes further, showing a live count per individual facet option ("5 miles (11)"), the strongest single pattern observed, though it requires real wired counts Solen does not yet confirm having. Mechanic for Solen: the Angebote filter sheet's commit button should read "N Ergebnisse anzeigen" style, restating the live count, not a bare "Anwenden"; cap visible top-level facet chips to what fits one unscrolled row at the 375px floor (grounded in the existing TabPill component's measured width, exact count set by the Taste-Lab probe, not invented here); overflow goes behind a single "Mehr Filter" disclosure, an existing progressive-disclosure practice (RATIONALE.md line 705) newly given a search-specific trigger condition.

Tension flagged, not applied: several of the real-app filter-chip references use saturated colored fills for selected state (Fresha's purple/blue applied-filter pills, Beli's teal count badges, Airwallex, N26 dark mode, OpenSea). This directly conflicts with Solen's locked selected-state law (calm gray `bg-s-bg-sunken`, never a colored or black fill). Noting the conflict for visibility; it does not reopen the lock, Solen's filter pills stay gray-sunken-selected regardless of what these apps do.

**Query reformulation is the normal path, not the failure path (T2, Bates 1989 berrypicking model).** Users rarely resolve intent in one query, they read a few results, then narrow or broaden. Mechanic: changing a facet or the search term must never force a full navigation reload that loses scroll position or the prior result set's context, the UI should read as adjusting a live view, not restarting a search. Real apps split into two families here (CONV, N26 and Airwallex instant-apply on tap with no button, versus the button-with-live-count family listed above); the button-with-live-count family is dominant specifically among booking/commerce apps, which is Solen's category, so it is the better-fit default, not a forced choice.

**Zero-result and low-result states need a named, structural recovery path, not a dead end (T3, Baymard Institute no-results research, reinforced by very strong real-app convergence, CONV across 12+ apps sampled).** Baymard's directional research says effective recovery needs concrete next actions, not generic tips like "check your spelling", which are largely ignored. Real-app sampling across TheFork, Walmart, Too Good To Go, Tabby, Google Drive, Wise, and ClassPass confirms one near-universal shape: icon/illustration, a bold short headline naming the filters (not the content) as the cause, one line of grey subtext, and exactly one primary single-tap recovery CTA that relaxes the most restrictive facet ("Kein Ergebnis fuer X, Y anzeigen" style, never a bare "keine Ergebnisse"). ClassPass adds a second, non-destructive recovery path ("Add categories") alongside the hard reset. HelloFresh is the strongest example in the sample: rather than a bare apology, it keeps a "Most recent recipes" fallback content section visible below the empty message, so the user is never on a true dead end, this is the aspirational ceiling for a Solen zero-result state, not just the copy floor. Below the hard-zero threshold, prefer ClassPass's softer technique for merely sparse results: keep the day-strip or facet state visible and add a relabeling header ("Andere Tage verfügbar" style) rather than replacing the results with an empty state at all. This is the search-specific instance of Solen's existing generic no-dead-ends copy law (RATIONALE.md line 807, Yifrah); the addition here is that search needs a STRUCTURAL recovery action (a tappable relax-filter control, or a relabeled fallback set), not just recovery COPY.

**Result-row scanning is top-left-weighted, with a caveat (T2, Nielsen 2006 F-pattern eye-tracking, n=232, explicitly a fallback pattern the source itself says appears when a page lacks structure; later independent eye-tracking work has questioned how universal the pattern is across layouts).** On an unstructured list this predicts where attention concentrates; Solen's cards are NOT unstructured (photo-led, named hierarchy per LOCKFILE card grammar), so the F-pattern does not override the existing card recipe, but it does set a placement rule for any NEW scannable text added to a result row: the single fact most likely to differentiate one result from its neighbors in a filtered list (the fact the user filtered ON, such as the matched service or the active promo) reads best placed early/top in the card's text block, not appended after price.

**Watch, do not build: natural-language / AI-generated search (T3, directional only, three data points).** Fabric ("Search with AI"), Todoist ("Filter Assist"), and Etsy (conversational "Reply or search") show an emerging pattern of natural-language or AI-assisted query generation, but it is three current apps, not a saturated convention, and it is a structural addition Solen has not scoped. This is flagged for future awareness only; it does not belong in a first mockup and conflicts with nothing locked, because nothing about it is being adopted here.

**Boundary.** This domain covers the PERCEPTUAL and INTERACTION mechanics of finding something (facet legibility, live-count commitment, reformulation continuity, recovery structure, scan placement). It explicitly does NOT cover: which filters Solen offers, single-select vs multi-select policy, the AND-combine backend contract, or ranking/personalization logic, those are locked product/backend decisions living in project memory and fable-backend, not perceptual law, and none of them are reopened here. Choice-count and option-overload psychology stay in PSYCHOLOGY.md law 11 (comparability-over-trimming, T1 cross-reference, d approx 0.02), this domain cross-references it rather than duplicating it, do not re-derive an overload argument here.

Taste-Lab probe design (for calibrating the facet-row-count and recovery-structure defaults against real Solen surfaces, since none of the numbers above are locked): Probe 1, show two versions of the Angebote filter bar at 375px, one with top-level facets fit to one unscrolled row plus a "Mehr Filter" disclosure (Fresha-style toolbar reference), one with a second wrapped row and no disclosure, measure first-facet-tap latency and ask which feels faster to scan. Probe 2, apply a facet combination that yields zero results, compare a bare "keine Ergebnisse" empty state against one offering a tappable relax-the-most-restrictive-facet action styled after the TheFork/Walmart/Wise convergent shape, ask which the user would tap first unprompted. Probe 3 (new, real-app-derived), for a low-but-nonzero result count, compare a hard empty-state replacement against ClassPass's relabel-as-fallback technique ("Andere Tage verfügbar" header, results stay visible), measure which one users perceive as still-useful versus a dead end. All three probes calibrate Solen-specific numeric or copy thresholds; the underlying directional claims (structural recovery beats copy-only, legible facets beat exhaustive facets, live-count commitment beats blind commitment) are already T2/T3/CONV-sourced above and are not what the probes test.

synth.taste_lab_probe: Three-part probe, all calibrating Solen-specific thresholds, none testing the underlying directional claims (already T2/T3/CONV sourced). Probe 1, facet-row-count threshold: at 375px width, compare the Angebote filter bar fit to one unscrolled row with a "Mehr Filter" disclosure (Fresha-toolbar reference shape) against a version that wraps to a second row with no disclosure; measure first-facet-tap latency and ask which feels faster to scan. Probe 2, recovery-path structure: apply a facet combination that yields zero results; compare a bare "keine Ergebnisse" empty state against one offering a tappable relax-the-most-restrictive-facet action styled after the convergent TheFork/Walmart/Wise shape; ask which the user would tap first, unprompted. Probe 3, sparse-result relabeling: for a low-but-nonzero result count, compare a hard empty-state replacement against ClassPass's relabel-as-fallback technique (results stay visible under an "Andere Tage verfügbar" style header); measure which one users perceive as still-useful versus a dead end.

myths_caught: "70 percent link-first / 30 percent search-first" attributed to Katz and Byrne 2003 (cited by NN/g) is FABRICATED/UNSUPPORTED. Traced the actual paper (Katz, M.A. and Byrne, M.D., "Effects of Scent and Breadth on Use of Site-Specific Search on E-Commerce Web Sites," ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction 10(3), 2003, pp.198-220) via a secondary summary (humanlinkllc.com): its real finding is that the study "found a wide distribution of searching and browsing behavior across sites and users" -- a spread, not a fixed 70/30 split. Could not confirm NN/g cites this number either: WebFetch of nngroup.com/articles/search-not-enough/ found no mention of Katz/Byrne or any 70/30 figure, and nngroup.com/articles/converting-search-navigation/ 404s. This is the classic pattern the myth_screen exists to catch: a real, correctly-named paper wearing an invented precise statistic. Downgraded and softened in verified_addition -- the qualitative claim (search and browse are mixed, not a fixed user-type split) survives on the real paper's actual finding; the 70/30 number does not.
verified.residual_risks: Owner-decision items: (1) the tension flagged in the draft is real and unresolved -- several referenced apps (Fresha, Beli, Airwallex, N26 dark mode, OpenSea) use saturated colored fills for selected filter state, which conflicts with Solen's locked gray-sunken-selected law; this is correctly NOT applied here, but belongs in QUESTIONS.md as a named tension, not silently dropped. (2) The Zocdoc per-option live-count pattern ("5 miles (11)") is confirmed as the single strongest real pattern found, but it requires real wired per-facet counts on Solen's Angebote backend that are not confirmed to exist; before this becomes a mockup default, someone needs to confirm the AND-combine query can cheaply return per-option counts without N+1 queries. (3) Minor unconfirmed detail: my own live fetch of fresha.com/search (default/no-filters state) showed toolbar pill labels as "Venues / Best match / Price / Options / Type" and no visible result-count line, which does not exactly reproduce the draft's specific quoted "21 venues nearby" text or its 4-pill labeling -- plausibly a different search/filter state than what the original researcher captured, not necessarily wrong, but not independently reproduced either. Treat the compound-chip search bar and pill-filter-toolbar shape as solid (matches my fetch); treat the exact quoted count copy as unverified. (4) Not independently re-checked this pass: the specific quoted commit-copy for eBay, Alan, FotMob, Glassdoor, Vivino, Shopee, TheFork, Walmart, Tabby, and the Fabric/Todoist/Etsy AI-search claim. Spot-checks on Zocdoc ("Show 418 results", "5 miles (11)"), ClassPass ("Available on other days"), HelloFresh ("Most recent recipes" fallback), and Booksy (8-tile category grid) all matched the draft precisely via live Mobbin/WebFetch lookups, which raises confidence in the rest of the CONV set, but that is inference from a sample, not a full re-verification.

claim_verdicts.claim: Users split into search-dominant and link-dominant types; 70 percent started a task by clicking a link, 30 percent started with search (Katz and Byrne 2003, cited by NN/g).
claim_verdicts.note: Paper is real (ACM TOCHI 10(3), 2003) and does study search-vs-menu navigation, but its actual reported finding is 'a wide distribution of searching and browsing behavior across sites and users,' not a 70/30 split. Could not find this number in any live NN/g article. Cut the number; keep the qualitative claim on the real paper's actual finding.

claim_verdicts.claim: Hierarchical faceted search interfaces should avoid empty result sets, show item counts before a facet is applied, and keep filter state visible and reversible (Hearst 2006, SIGIR faceted search workshop).
claim_verdicts.note: Marti Hearst is a real, highly-cited Berkeley HCI researcher; her Flamenco faceted-search project and this exact paper title are canonical in the IR/HCI literature. PDF resolved at her own research URL (291KB, real file) though text extraction failed; treated as verified on paper identity and field consensus, not full-text re-read.

claim_verdicts.claim: Real-world information seeking rarely resolves in one query; searchers iterate through reformulations (Bates 1989, berrypicking).
claim_verdicts.note: Canonical, extremely well-established IR paper; not independently re-fetched this pass but confidence is very high given how foundational and unambiguously real this citation is in the field.

claim_verdicts.claim: 2006 NN/g eye-tracking study found an F-shaped scanning pattern, n=232, described as a fallback tied to low content structure rather than universal.
claim_verdicts.note: Directly confirmed via WebFetch of nngroup.com/articles/f-shaped-pattern-reading-web-content-discovered/: exact quote 'we recorded how 232 users looked at thousands of Web pages.' The 'fallback, not universal' caveat is also directly supported by the live article, which names layer-cake, spotted, marking, bypassing, and commitment as alternate patterns.

claim_verdicts.claim: Effective zero-results recovery needs concrete next actions, not generic tips like checking spelling; a large share of e-commerce sites still ship a dead-end no-results page (Baymard Institute).
claim_verdicts.note: Confirmed live at baymard.com/blog/no-results-page: 5 named strategies, explicit statement that generic tips are rarely read/applied, and 'nearly 50% of sites fail to provide effective recovery.' Draft's softened framing ('large share') is consistent with this and correctly avoids over-precision.

claim_verdicts.claim: Choice-overload effect is weak/non-replicating at the population level (d approx 0.02); fix is comparability/grouping, not catalog trimming.
claim_verdicts.note: Matches the exact ALLOWED substitute phrasing in the myth_screen table for the jam-study myth. Correctly used as a cross-reference to PSYCHOLOGY.md law 11 rather than re-derived or re-sourced here -- compliant.

claim_verdicts.claim: Zocdoc's filter-sheet commit button restates the live result count before commit (e.g. 'Show 418 results'), and its distance facet shows a live per-option count in parentheses (e.g. '5 miles (11)').
claim_verdicts.note: Directly spot-verified this session via Mobbin screen search: real Zocdoc screenshots show exactly 'Show 418 results', 'Show 356 results', 'Show 21 results' commit buttons and '5 miles (11)', '25 miles (106)' style per-option counts. Precise match to the draft's claim.

claim_verdicts.claim: Zero-result recovery converges on icon/headline naming filters as cause + subtext + single CTA across TheFork, Walmart, Too Good To Go, Tabby, Google Drive, Wise, ClassPass; HelloFresh adds a 'Most recent recipes' fallback section instead of a bare apology.
claim_verdicts.note: Spot-verified via Mobbin for Too Good To Go ('No stores matching your filters' + 'Clear filters'), Google Drive ('No matching results' + 'Clear filters'), Wise ('Your filters have returned no results' + 'Clear filters'), and HelloFresh (exact match: 'Sorry, we couldn't find recipes that match your filters' + tips + a visible 'Most recent recipes' section below). TheFork, Walmart, and Tabby not individually re-checked this pass but the convergent shape is now confirmed across 6+ independently sampled apps including 3 not even in the draft's list (GitHub, Skyscanner, Quizlet all showed the same shape), which reinforces the pattern claim.

claim_verdicts.claim: ClassPass relabels sparse results under an 'Available on other days' header instead of wiping the screen to an empty state, with the day-strip staying visible.
claim_verdicts.note: Directly confirmed via Mobbin: real ClassPass screens show a visible day-strip (Today/Wed 18/Thu 19...) with an 'Available on other days' section header and results still rendered below it, exactly as described.

claim_verdicts.claim: Booksy leads with a browse-first icon-tile category grid (roughly 8 primary categories); Fresha leads with a compound search-state chip and a pill-filter toolbar.
claim_verdicts.note: Booksy confirmed via live WebFetch: 8 primary category tiles (Hair, Barber, Nails, Skin care, Brows and lashes, Massage, Makeup, Wellness and spa) plus a 'More...' expansion, matching the draft closely. Fresha's compound-chip search bar and pill-filter-toolbar shape also confirmed via live WebFetch, though the specific quoted copy ('Hair & styling | Tomorrow | Current location', '21 venues nearby', pill labels 'all-filters/Sort by/Max price/Venue type') was not exactly reproduced in my fetch of the default (no-filters) state -- likely a different search state, not necessarily fabricated, but not independently confirmed as quoted.

claim_verdicts.claim: Treatwell leads with a treatment-level trending/social discovery rail ('What is hot on socials') ahead of any typed query.
claim_verdicts.note: Not independently re-fetched this pass due to tool-budget constraints; not implausible given Treatwell's known product design, but unverified this session -- treat as the weakest-confirmed claim in the competitor-comparison set.

claim_verdicts.claim: Natural-language/AI-generated search input is an emerging pattern in a small number of current apps (Fabric 'Search with AI', Todoist 'Filter Assist', Etsy conversational 'Reply or search') -- three data points, not a saturated convention.
claim_verdicts.note: Not independently re-verified this pass. Already appropriately hedged in the draft as directional-only, explicitly 'watch, do not build,' and does not touch any Solen mechanic -- low risk even if one of the three examples is imprecise.

claim_verdicts.claim: Tension: several referenced apps (Fresha, Beli, Airwallex, N26 dark mode, OpenSea) use saturated colored fills for selected filter/facet state, conflicting with Solen's locked gray-sunken-selected law.
claim_verdicts.note: Not independently re-verified app-by-app this pass, but the general claim (many apps use colored selected-filter fills, which is exactly why Solen's LOCKFILE has to explicitly override the 'obvious' pattern with a gray-fill law) is directionally credible and correctly handled: flagged as a tension, not silently adopted, and not used to reopen the lock.

Katz and Byrne's 2003 e-commerce search study (ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction 10(3), pp.198-220) found a wide distribution of searching and browsing behavior across sites and users, not a fixed split between search-first and link-first types (T2, correcting an earlier draft that misattributed a specific "70/30" figure to this paper; the paper does not report that number and no live NN/g article was found citing it either). Real-app confirmation shows no industry consensus on the search-vs-browse balance itself: Fresha leads with a compound search-state chip (search-first), Booksy leads with a browse-first icon-tile category grid (8 primary categories confirmed live), Treatwell leads with a trending-treatments discovery rail (browse-first with search retained in the header, not independently re-verified this pass). This domain does not pick a winner among the three, it governs the mechanics UNDER whichever balance Solen's own traffic mix justifies, and under Solen's existing locked search and Angebote-filter behavior (single-select owner lock, AND-combine backend, already project fact, not repeated or reopened here).

**Facet state stays visible and legible, ideally with a live outcome count (T2 Hearst 2006, reinforced by strong real-app convergence, CONV, directly spot-verified this pass).** Hearst's design recommendations call for showing counts before a facet is applied, keeping the current filter state visible and reversible, and never landing on an unrecoverable empty set. Current shipping apps confirm this is not just academic advice: a live Mobbin lookup of Zocdoc's filter sheet shows exactly this pattern in production, commit buttons reading "Show 418 results", "Show 356 results", "Show 21 results" restating the outcome before the user commits, so the user chooses a result, not a guess. Zocdoc goes further, showing a live count per individual facet option ("5 miles (11)", "25 miles (106)"), the strongest single pattern observed and directly confirmed, though it requires real wired per-option counts Solen does not yet confirm having on the Angebote backend (flagged as an open dependency, not assumed). Mechanic for Solen: the Angebote filter sheet's commit button should read "N Ergebnisse anzeigen" style, restating the live count, not a bare "Anwenden"; cap visible top-level facet chips to what fits one unscrolled row at the 375px floor (grounded in the existing TabPill component's measured width, exact count set by the Taste-Lab probe below, not invented here); overflow goes behind a single "Mehr Filter" disclosure, an existing progressive-disclosure practice (RATIONALE.md line 705) newly given a search-specific trigger condition.

Tension flagged, not applied: several real-app filter-chip references use saturated colored fills for selected state (Fresha's purple/blue applied-filter pills, Beli's teal count badges, Airwallex, N26 dark mode, OpenSea). This directly conflicts with Solen's locked selected-state law (calm gray `bg-s-bg-sunken`, never a colored or black fill). Noting the conflict for visibility as a QUESTIONS.md candidate; it does not reopen the lock, Solen's filter pills stay gray-sunken-selected regardless of what these apps do.

**Query reformulation is the normal path, not the failure path (T2, Bates 1989 berrypicking model).** Users rarely resolve intent in one query, they read a few results, then narrow or broaden. Mechanic: changing a facet or the search term must never force a full navigation reload that loses scroll position or the prior result set's context, the UI should read as adjusting a live view, not restarting a search. Real apps split into two families here (CONV, N26 and Airwallex instant-apply on tap with no button, versus the button-with-live-count family confirmed above); the button-with-live-count family is dominant specifically among booking/commerce apps, which is Solen's category, so it is the better-fit default, not a forced choice.

**Zero-result and low-result states need a named, structural recovery path, not a dead end (T3, Baymard Institute no-results research, directly confirmed live, reinforced by strong real-app convergence, CONV, spot-verified across 6+ apps).** Baymard's live research page confirms its own directional claim: generic tips like "check your spelling" are rarely read or applied, and roughly half of e-commerce sites still ship an ineffective recovery page. Real-app sampling confirms one near-universal shape, directly verified this pass for Too Good To Go ("No stores matching your filters" / "Clear filters"), Google Drive ("No matching results" / "Clear filters"), and Wise ("Your filters have returned no results" / "Clear filters"), and the same shape additionally turned up unprompted in GitHub, Skyscanner, and Quizlet: icon/illustration, a bold short headline naming the filters (not the content) as the cause, one line of grey subtext, and exactly one primary single-tap recovery CTA that relaxes the most restrictive facet, never a bare "keine Ergebnisse". HelloFresh is the strongest example, directly confirmed: rather than a bare apology ("Sorry, we couldn't find recipes that match your filters"), it keeps a "Most recent recipes" fallback content section visible below the empty message, so the user is never on a true dead end, this is the aspirational ceiling for a Solen zero-result state, not just the copy floor. Below the hard-zero threshold, prefer ClassPass's softer technique for merely sparse results, directly confirmed: keep the day-strip visible and add a relabeling header ("Available on other days" in the real app, "Andere Tage verfügbar" style in German) rather than replacing the results with an empty state at all. This is the search-specific instance of Solen's existing generic no-dead-ends copy law (RATIONALE.md line 807, Yifrah); the addition here is that search needs a STRUCTURAL recovery action (a tappable relax-filter control, or a relabeled fallback set), not just recovery COPY.

**Result-row scanning is top-left-weighted, with a caveat (T2, Nielsen 2006 F-pattern eye-tracking, n=232, confirmed directly this pass; the source itself, not just a later critique, says the pattern is a fallback that appears "when there are no strong cues to attract the eyes towards meaningful information" and names layer-cake, spotted, marking, bypassing, and commitment as other common patterns).** On an unstructured list this predicts where attention concentrates; Solen's cards are NOT unstructured (photo-led, named hierarchy per LOCKFILE card grammar), so the F-pattern does not override the existing card recipe, but it does set a placement rule for any NEW scannable text added to a result row: the single fact most likely to differentiate one result from its neighbors in a filtered list (the fact the user filtered ON, such as the matched service or the active promo) reads best placed early/top in the card's text block, not appended after price.

**Watch, do not build: natural-language / AI-generated search (T3, directional only, three data points, not independently re-verified this pass).** Fabric ("Search with AI"), Todoist ("Filter Assist"), and Etsy (conversational "Reply or search") are cited as an emerging pattern of natural-language or AI-assisted query generation, but it is three current apps, not a saturated convention, and it is a structural addition Solen has not scoped. This is flagged for future awareness only; it does not belong in a first mockup and conflicts with nothing locked, because nothing about it is being adopted here.

**Boundary.** This domain covers the PERCEPTUAL and INTERACTION mechanics of finding something (facet legibility, live-count commitment, reformulation continuity, recovery structure, scan placement). It explicitly does NOT cover: which filters Solen offers, single-select vs multi-select policy, the AND-combine backend contract, or ranking/personalization logic, those are locked product/backend decisions living in project memory and fable-backend, not perceptual law, and none of them are reopened here. Choice-count and option-overload psychology stay in PSYCHOLOGY.md law 11 (comparability-over-trimming, T1 cross-reference, d approx 0.02), this domain cross-references it rather than duplicating it, do not re-derive an overload argument here.

Taste-Lab probe design (for calibrating the facet-row-count and recovery-structure defaults against real Solen surfaces, since none of the numbers above are locked): Probe 1, show two versions of the Angebote filter bar at 375px, one with top-level facets fit to one unscrolled row plus a "Mehr Filter" disclosure (Fresha-style toolbar reference), one with a second wrapped row and no disclosure, measure first-facet-tap latency and ask which feels faster to scan. Probe 2, apply a facet combination that yields zero results, compare a bare "keine Ergebnisse" empty state against one offering a tappable relax-the-most-restrictive-facet action styled after the confirmed convergent shape (Too Good To Go / Google Drive / Wise), ask which the user would tap first unprompted. Probe 3, for a low-but-nonzero result count, compare a hard empty-state replacement against ClassPass's relabel-as-fallback technique ("Andere Tage verfügbar" header, results stay visible), measure which one users perceive as still-useful versus a dead end. All three probes calibrate Solen-specific numeric or copy thresholds; the underlying directional claims (structural recovery beats copy-only, legible facets beat exhaustive facets, live-count commitment beats blind commitment) are already T2/T3/CONV-sourced above, independently confirmed live this pass for the Zocdoc, ClassPass, HelloFresh, Too Good To Go, Google Drive, Wise, and Booksy examples, and are not what the probes test.
